title: WHY DID JESUS CALL SOME PEOPLE “WORKERS OF LAWLESSNESS”?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS CALL SOME PEOPLE “WORKERS OF LAWLESSNESS”?
There are few sentences in Scripture more terrifying than this one.
“Then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness.’” (Matthew 7:23)
Not people who openly hated God.
The people hearing those words were religious.
They used the name of Jesus.
For many readers, this passage creates a deep and unsettling question:
How can someone spend years around spiritual things and still hear Christ say, “I never knew you”?
The answer reaches far deeper than church attendance, ministry activity, theological knowledge, or outward religious appearance.
It reaches into the very heart of what it means to truly know Jesus Christ.
The Crowd That Thought They Were Safe
The warning appears near the conclusion of Jesus' Sermon on the Mount.
This was not spoken to the worst people in society.
It was spoken to people who believed they were on the right path.
“Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven...” (Matthew 7:21)
It reflects urgency, passion, sincerity, and even emotional devotion.
These individuals genuinely believed they belonged to Him.
When judgment came, they immediately began listing their spiritual accomplishments.
“Did we not prophesy in Your name?”
“Did we not cast out demons in Your name?”
“Did we not do many mighty works in Your name?”
Every defense they offer centers on what they did.
Their confidence rested entirely on their religious resume.
The Most Chilling Words in the Passage
“I knew you and then forgot you.”
At no point did a genuine saving relationship exist.
Throughout Scripture, “knowing” often refers to intimate relationship rather than mere intellectual awareness.
Jesus is exposing a devastating reality:
It is possible to know about Him without truly knowing Him.
But knowing Christ is something entirely different.

οἱ ἐργαζόμενοι τὴν ἀνομίαν
(hoi ergazomenoi tēn anomian)
“Living as though God's authority does not matter.”
This does not simply describe people who occasionally sinned.
Lawlessness describes a heart that wants the benefits of Christ without submission to Christ.
A person who wants salvation without surrender.
Jesus is not condemning weak believers.
The Jewish audience would have immediately connected this idea to the Hebrew Scriptures.
The Hebrew concept behind lawlessness is often expressed through words such as:
“Depart from me, all you workers of evil.”
Jesus intentionally echoes Old Testament judgment language.
His audience would have recognized it immediately.
The issue was never merely breaking rules.
The issue was a heart fundamentally opposed to God's reign.
Perhaps the most shocking element of the passage is that miracles are mentioned.
Many modern readers assume supernatural activity automatically proves spiritual authenticity.
The Bible repeatedly shows that supernatural power alone is not evidence of salvation.
The Beast's system in Revelation performs signs.
Even Judas Iscariot ministered among the Twelve.
Only transformed hearts reveal genuine discipleship.
Jesus never taught that gifts are the highest evidence of salvation.
Just a few verses earlier He said:
“You will recognize them by their fruits.”
The Hidden Danger of Religious Performance
One reason this passage hits so hard is because it exposes a temptation hiding inside every human heart.
We naturally want something we can point to.
We want evidence that makes us feel secure.
But salvation has never been based on performance.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God.” (Ephesians 2:8)
The rejected people in Matthew 7 stood before Christ holding their accomplishments.
The redeemed stand before Christ holding His righteousness.
The Question Every Believer Must Ask
This passage is not intended to create panic among genuine Christians.
It is intended to destroy false assurance.
“Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith.” (2 Corinthians 13:5)
Am I repenting when I sin?
Is there evidence of His transforming work in my life?
Perfection is not the evidence of salvation.
But sheep still follow the Shepherd.
The Gospel Hidden Inside the Warning
Ironically, one of the strongest warnings in Scripture contains one of the strongest invitations.
The solution is not more religious activity.
The solution is a genuine relationship with the Savior.
The same Jesus who warned about false disciples also said:
“Whoever comes to Me I will never cast out.” (John 6:37)
The people of Matthew 7 trusted their works.
The people of Matthew 7 stood before Jesus presenting achievements.
The believer stands before Jesus covered by grace.
The people of Matthew 7 wanted His power.
Perhaps that is why this passage continues to shake hearts across generations.
Because deep down, every one of us knows how easy it is to build a public image while neglecting a private relationship with God.
The greatest tragedy is not failing publicly.
The greatest tragedy is appearing spiritual while remaining unknown by Christ.
One day every title, every platform, every achievement, every applause, every ministry success, and every earthly accomplishment will disappear.
Have you ever struggled with relying on what you do for God more than what Christ has done for you?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
The most dangerous distance from Jesus is not rebellion that knows it is lost—it is religion that believes it is already home.
